title: Many Who Are First Will Be Last, and the Last First
paragraphs:
Many Who Are First Will Be Last, and the Last First
The Shocking Words of Jesus That Still Turn Human Pride Upside Down
What if one sentence from Jesus could dismantle everything the world taught you about success?
What if the people everyone admires are not necessarily the ones Heaven celebrates?
What if the people who feel forgotten, overlooked, broken, ashamed, disqualified, and pushed to the edges of society are far closer to the heart of God than they realize?
Jesus looked at a world obsessed with status, power, recognition, wealth, influence, titles, achievements, and applause, and He said something that sounded almost impossible:
“But many who are first will be last, and the last first.” (Matthew 19:30)
Then He said it again in Matthew 20:16 after telling a parable that left many listeners uncomfortable:
“So the last will be first, and the first last.”

For centuries these words have challenged kings, religious leaders, scholars, business owners, celebrities, politicians, and ordinary people alike. They challenge us because they expose a truth we often try to avoid.
God does not measure greatness the way we do.
The Greek text of Matthew 19:30 reads:

πολλοὶ δὲ ἔσονται πρῶτοι ἔσχατοι καὶ ἔσχατοι πρῶτοι
polloi de esontai prōtoi eschatoi kai eschatoi prōtoi
Literally:
“Many will be first, last; and last, first.”
The emphasis is startlingly direct.
Those who appear first now may not remain first in God's Kingdom.
Those who appear last now may not remain last forever.
To understand what Jesus meant, we must understand the moment in which He spoke these words.

A wealthy young ruler had just approached Jesus asking what he must do to inherit eternal life. Outwardly, he seemed like the perfect candidate for God's favor. He was moral. Respected. Successful. Influential.
Yet when Jesus told him to surrender the thing he loved most—his wealth—the man walked away sorrowful because his possessions possessed him.
The disciples were stunned.
If someone that righteous and successful struggled to enter God's Kingdom, who could possibly be saved?
Peter then reminded Jesus that the disciples had left everything to follow Him.
It was in that context that Jesus declared:
“Many who are first will be last, and the last first.”
Jesus was not teaching that poverty automatically saves people or that wealth automatically condemns them. Scripture consistently rejects both ideas.
Instead, Jesus was exposing the danger of trusting in earthly status while neglecting complete dependence on God.
The Kingdom of God operates differently.
The world says:
Be seen.
Jesus says:
Be faithful.
The world says:
Promote yourself.
Jesus says:
Humble yourself.
The world says:
Climb higher.
Jesus says:
Serve lower.
The world says:
Make your name great.
Jesus says:
Follow Mine.
That truth becomes even more powerful when we look at the Hebrew mindset behind Scripture.
The Hebrew concept of humility is often connected to the word:
עָנָו (anav)
Meaning humble, lowly, dependent upon God.
Moses is described using this language in Numbers 12:3.
The humble are not people who think little of themselves.
They are people who think much of God.
Throughout the Bible, God repeatedly chooses the unexpected.
Abel over Cain.
Isaac over Ishmael.
Jacob over Esau.
Joseph over his older brothers.
David over his stronger brothers.
The shepherd boy over the giant.
The widow over the wealthy.
The tax collector over the self-righteous Pharisee.
Again and again, God demonstrates that His ways are not our ways.
The pattern reaches its climax in Jesus Himself.
The King of Kings entered the world not through a palace but through a manger.
The Creator of the universe washed feet.
The Lord of glory wore a crown of thorns.
The One worthy of all worship hung on a Roman cross.
Isaiah prophesied this centuries earlier:
“He was despised and rejected by men.” (Isaiah 53:3)
To the world, Jesus looked last.
To Heaven, Jesus was first.
And through His death and resurrection, He rewrote the story of humanity.
That is why our theme matters so deeply:
The Gospel itself is the greatest scandal-to-grace story ever told.
Peter denied Christ.
Paul persecuted Christians.
The woman caught in adultery expected condemnation.
The thief on the cross expected judgment.
Yet Jesus transformed their stories.
He still does.
Perhaps you know what it feels like to be last.
Last to be chosen.
Last to be noticed.
Last to be understood.
Last to be forgiven.
Last to believe your life could matter.
Maybe you've carried mistakes that still haunt you.
Maybe you've spent years pretending everything is fine while quietly falling apart.
Maybe you've watched others succeed while you wondered if God had forgotten your name.
Hear the words of Jesus carefully.
Being last in the eyes of the world does not mean you are last in the eyes of God.
The cross permanently destroyed that lie.
The Gospel announces that God's grace reaches farther than your failures, deeper than your wounds, and higher than your shame.
The Aramaic-speaking followers of Jesus would have understood something beautiful about this message.
When Jesus often addressed God as Father, the Aramaic word was:
ܐܒܐ (Abba)
A deeply personal expression of intimacy and trust.
Not merely a distant ruler.
A loving Father.
The God who sees the forgotten.
The God who pursues the lost.
The God who welcomes prodigals home.
The God who specializes in rewriting stories.
That is why the Kingdom is filled with surprises.
The proud become humbled.
The broken become healed.
The guilty become forgiven.
The lost become found.
The last become first.
And the first become last.
Not because God is unfair.
Because God sees what human eyes often miss.
He sees motives.
He sees hearts.
He sees secret sacrifices.
He sees hidden faithfulness.
He sees the tears nobody else notices.
Every prayer whispered in loneliness.
Every act of obedience nobody applauded.
Every moment you chose Christ when nobody was watching.
Nothing escapes His attention.
One day, Heaven's scoreboard will be revealed.
And many people we barely noticed on earth may shine with extraordinary glory because they quietly lived for Jesus.
This truth should both comfort and challenge us.
Comfort us when we feel overlooked.
Challenge us when we seek recognition more than faithfulness.
The question is not whether people think we are first.
The question is whether Christ is truly first.
Because in the end, eternity is not about who accumulated the most applause.
It is about who surrendered most completely to Jesus.
If this message spoke to your heart, do not keep it to yourself.
Your testimony may become the encouragement someone else desperately needs today.
You can learn more here:
Salvation is by grace alone through faith in Christ alone.
But supporting Gospel-centered ministry helps spread biblical truth to more people who need to hear that Jesus still saves, forgives, restores, heals, and transforms lives today.
And maybe that is the deepest meaning behind Jesus' words.
The world writes people off.
Jesus rewrites them.
The world labels them.
Jesus redeems them.
The world remembers the scandal.
Jesus reveals the grace.
The people everyone counted out may become living evidence of God's glory.
Because when Jesus takes hold of a life, the ending is no longer determined by the beginning.
The last chapter belongs to Him.
And He is still writing.
The people the world calls forgotten are often the very people Heaven is preparing to reveal.
